claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite is prone to phase separation during high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
The untreated W–Cu composite is prone to interfacial void formation during high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
Introducing approximately 3 wt% Ni uniformly into the W–Cu composite will mitigate phase separation.
Introducing approximately 3 wt% Ni uniformly into the W–Cu composite will mitigate interfacial void formation.
Ni introduced at a trace level will segregate preferentially to W/Cu interfaces.
Interfacial Ni acts as a wetting agent at W/Cu interfaces.
Interfacial Ni enhances adhesion between W and Cu.
Interfacial Ni improves structural continuity across W/Cu interfaces.
Ni reduces the interfacial-energy mismatch between W and Cu.
Ni inhibits diffusion-driven phase separation in the W–Cu composite.
Ni inhibits void nucleation at W/Cu interfaces.
Suppression of phase separation and void nucleation preserves the thermal-conduction network during cyclic thermal and irradiation stresses.
The Ni-doped composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable untreated W–Cu composite.
Improved interfacial bonding and reduced void formation are responsible for the predicted increase in thermal conductivity.
The proposed effect applies to composites made by conventional powder-metallurgy and sintering routes.
The proposed effect applies during thermal exposure or cycling in the approximate range of 600–800 °C with concurrent irradiation relevant to plasma-facing applications.
Applicability beyond approximately 800 °C or beyond the contemplated irradiation-dose regime has not been established.
